title: Repairing the world
hookLine: Jews across communities speak of repairing the world through justice and service

cards: Two Hebrew words turn up on banners at food drives, on youth group T-shirts, in sermons about hunger, refugees, the climate. Tikkun olam. Repairing the world.
Some people hear a modern slogan, something a committee came up with.

But these words are old, and the road they took to a T-shirt runs through a law court, a prayer said at the end of services, and a mystical teaching about scattered light. They have more layers than the banner shows.

teach.h: A LOOPHOLE CLOSED IN A COURT.
teach.b: Tikkun means repairing, or setting right. Olam means world. The phrase appears in the Mishnah, in a chapter about divorce law, and it's surprisingly practical.
A husband who had sent his wife a divorce document could once cancel it before a court in another town, without her knowing. She might remarry, believing she was free, when she wasn't.

Rabban Gamliel the Elder put a stop to that, and the Mishnah gives the reason: for the repair of the world. The same reason is given for other rulings that close loopholes and protect people who could be harmed.
So the first layer is legal: fixing the rules so the vulnerable aren't left exposed. The second layer is prayer.

teach.h: A PRAYER FOR A WORLD SET RIGHT.
teach.b: The Aleinu, said at the end of services, looks toward a day when the world will be set right under the sovereignty of God. The third comes from the mystics of Safed.

In a teaching that tradition links to Rabbi Isaac Luria, divine light was scattered into the world in sparks, and each good deed and each commandment lifts a spark back up, so every small act helps mend something cosmic.

Then the modern layer, justice and service, with the Torah's line underneath: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." Communities lean on these layers differently. Some put social justice at the center.
Others say the commandments themselves, prayer, Shabbat, study, are how the world is repaired. Some hold both.
And the Mishnah adds a line from Rabbi Tarfon, in paraphrase: it isn't on you to finish the work, and you aren't free to walk away from it.

how: Jewish communities speak of tikkun olam in volunteering, giving and social justice work, in the Aleinu prayer said at the end of services, and in the teaching that the commandments themselves help set the world right; communities weigh these differently.

o: the world to come, promised after the Messiah
repairing the world, from old court rulings to justice
the Kabbalah's name for the world's first light

p: closed a loophole, to repair the world
not on you to finish the work

s: tikkun olam began as a modern activist slogan
the phrase appears in the Mishnah, as the reason for rulings that protect people.
the Aleinu, said at the end of services, looks toward a world set right
repair there is a hope as wide as the earth.

games.q: you're a judge. a husband can cancel a divorce in a court in another town, without his wife knowing. she may remarry believing she's free. what do you rule?
o: leave the law as it is; the procedure is valid.
stop the secret cancellation, for the repair of the world.
let each town's court decide for itself.
games.why: Rabban Gamliel the Elder stopped it, and the Mishnah gives the reason: for the repair of the world. the phrase begins as a way to protect someone who could be harmed.

practice: Let one broken thing in your neighborhood come to mind: a lonely neighbor, a short-handed food bank, a park full of litter, a child who needs help reading. Don't try to fix the whole world; Rabbi Tarfon already let you off that.
Picture one hour, one place, and yourself walking in the door, and if you pray, ask in your own words for strength for that hour.

wordCard.voice: Tikkun olam. Repairing the world: a court's reason for protecting the vulnerable, a prayer's hope, scattered sparks, and justice and service today. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: repair the world. Not all of it, and not alone. See you tomorrow.
